title: Mardi Gras
description: Holiday on the day before Ash Wednesday
wiki_lead:
Mardi Gras (UK: ; US: ), also known as Shrove Tuesday, is the final day of Carnival (also known as Shrovetide or Fastelavn); it thus falls on the day before the beginning of Lent on Ash Wednesday. Mardi Gras ([maʁdi ɡʁa]) is French for "Fat Tuesday", referring to it being the last day of consuming rich, fatty foods, most notably red meat, in preparation for the Christian fasting season of Lent, during which such foods are avoided.
Related popular practices are associated with Carnival celebrations before the fasting and religious obligations associated with the penitential season of Lent. In countries such as the United Kingdom, Mardi Gras is more usually known as Pancake Day or (traditionally) Shrove Tuesday, derived from the word shrive, meaning "to administer the sacrament of confession to; to absolve".

Mardi Gras (UK: ; US: ), also known as Shrove Tuesday, is the final day of Carnival (also known as Shrovetide or Fastelavn); it thus falls on the day before the beginning of Lent on Ash Wednesday. Mardi Gras ([maʁdi ɡʁa]) is French for "Fat Tuesday", referring to it being the last day of consuming rich, fatty foods, most notably red meat, in preparation for the Christian fasting season of Lent, during which such foods are avoided.
Related popular practices are associated with Carnival celebrations before the fasting and religious obligations associated with the penitential season of Lent. In countries such as the United Kingdom, Mardi Gras is more usually known as Pancake Day or (traditionally) Shrove Tuesday, derived from the word shrive, meaning "to administer the sacrament of confession to; to absolve".


Background
During the liturgical season of Lent, some Christians abstain from the consumption of certain foods such as meat, eggs, dairy products, and alcoholic beverages. Most Christian denominations observe the tradition of Lent; exceptions include many churches within the Anabaptist, Baptist, Methodist, and Reformed traditions. Shrovetide provided Christians with the opportunity to use up these foods prior to the start of the 40-day fasting season of Lent. 
Prior to the 6th century, Lent was normatively observed through the practice of the Black Fast, which enjoins fasting from food and liquids, with the allowance of one vegetarian meal and water after sunset. The tradition of pancake breakfasts during Shrovetide, as well as that of pancake races, owes itself to this practice of "using up the surplus eggs, milk and butter" prior to Lent. 
The specific tradition of eating pancakes is said to have roots in Slavic paganism, with this practice being co-opted into Christian ritual. Specifically the pancake was said to symbolise the returning of the sun as spring approached.
In many Christian parish churches, both Protestant and Roman Catholic, a popular Shrove Tuesday tradition is the ringing of the church bells (on this day, the toll is known as the Shriving Bell) "to call the faithful to confession before the solemn season of Lent" and for people to "begin frying their pancakes". As such, a hallmark of Shrovetide is the opportunity for a last round of merrymaking associated with Mardis Gras before the start of the somber Lenten season. The last day of Shrovetide, Mardi Gras (Fat Tuesday), is named as such "because people felt bloated having eaten up all the rich foods before Lent" in order to prepare for the coming season of repentance.


Traditions
The festival season varies from city to city; Mardis Gras often refers to the last day of Shrovetide (or Fastelavn or Carnival), thus being synonymous with Shrove Tuesday. Some traditions, such as the one in New Orleans, Louisiana, consider Mardi Gras to stretch the entire period from Twelfth Night (the last night of Christmas which begins Epiphany) to Ash Wednesday. grok_lead: Mardi Gras, French for "Fat Tuesday," is a Christian holiday and cultural festival celebrated on the Tuesday before Ash Wednesday, serving as the culmination of the Carnival season and the final opportunity for indulgence before the Lenten period of fasting and penance leading to Easter. It is observed worldwide, particularly in regions with Catholic traditions, including Europe, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Originating from ancient pagan spring and fertility rites, including Roman festivals like Saturnalia and Lupercalia, the tradition evolved in medieval Europe through celebrations in Rome, Venice, and France before being brought to the Americas by European colonists. In Louisiana, it reflects a multicultural blend of European, African, and Caribbean influences, transforming into a vibrant public spectacle characterized by elaborate parades, masked balls, and communal feasting. The first recorded Mardi Gras in North America occurred on March 3, 1699, when French explorers led by Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville celebrated near present-day New Orleans by naming a point of land "Pointe du Mardi Gras." Formal celebrations began in 1703 in Mobile, Alabama, under French colonial rule, with the first organized parade and masked ball taking place there in 1711. By the 1730s, public festivities had emerged in New Orleans, founded in 1718, evolving from elegant private balls in the 1740s to street processions in the late 1830s that featured flambeaux carriers and cowbell-ringing marchers. The modern structure of Mardi Gras solidified in the mid-19th century with the founding of secret societies known as krewes, starting with the Mistick Krewe of Comus in 1857, which introduced illuminated floats, themed parades, and opulent masked balls. New Orleans remains the epicenter of Mardi Gras celebrations, designated a legal holiday in Louisiana in 1875, drawing millions annually for its week-long Carnival season that begins on January 6 ( Twelfth Night) and peaks on Fat Tuesday. Key traditions include parades organized by over 70 krewes, such as the Rex organization established in 1872, which introduced the official Mardi Gras colors of purple, green, and goldâtheir symbolism of justice, faith, and power defined in 1892. Revelers participate by "throwing" beads, doubloons, and other trinkets from floats, while masking allows for social inversion and anonymity during street parties. Culinary staples like king cake â a ring-shaped pastry with a hidden baby figurine symbolizing the Christ child âadd to the festivities, with the finder of the baby traditionally hosting the next celebration. Beyond New Orleans, variations persist in places like Mobile and rural Louisiana 's Courir de Mardi Gras, where costumed riders on horseback chase chickens in a chaotic, medieval-inspired pursuit.
